## Idle and Thackley

_Bradford council, West Yorkshire; postponed from 7th May following the death of outgoing Liberal Democrat councillor Jeanette Sunderland, who was seeking re-election._

There is a suburb of Bradford called Idle. It has a Working Men’s Club.

In case you don’t believe me, here’s a photograph.

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!BEsJ!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0988bade-961b-44ca-b898-2eb6b4b509d5_600x800.webp)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!BEsJ!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0988bade-961b-44ca-b898-2eb6b4b509d5_600x800.webp)

Partly because of its name, the Idle Working Men’s Club is bucking the national trend for licensed premises to struggle. I am informed that it has a seven-year waiting list for membership. And it’s known in quizland not just for its name but as a venue: earlier this month the Idle WMC hosted the end-of-season finals night for the Airedale Quiz League, with the venue’s resident team Colonel’s Bogies losing the cup final by a single point.

(I also notice from the results that the “Airebrain” singles competition was won by quizzer Scott Dalgliesh ahead of a star-studded field. Of the other three finalists, Diane Hallagan (who finished second) is one of the four people who have beaten me on BBC _Mastermind_, Joseph Krol (3rd) was a fearsome quizbowl player in his university days who captained the Corpus Christi Cambridge team in the 2017-18 series of _University Challenge_, and 4th-placed Barry Simmons may well be known to readers as one of TV’s _Eggheads_. His list of defeated contestants on _Eggheads_ includes, er, me.)

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!4CHi!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F36e7d765-901a-4983-aa50-a977bea0d0e4_554x453.webp)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!4CHi!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F36e7d765-901a-4983-aa50-a977bea0d0e4_554x453.webp)

Idle lies on high ground to the north-east of Bradford city centre, clinging to the side of a steep slope down towards the River Aire and the Leeds and Liverpool Canal. Thackley is on lower ground to the north of Idle, although still high enough for the Airedale railway line to need to pass beneath it in a tunnel. The main road from Bradford to Harrogate crosses the Aire valley at Apperley Bridge, whose railway station reopened in 2015 and has half-hourly trains to Leeds and Bradford city centres.

The local authority here is Bradford council, which is now hung after Labour lost control of the district in May’s elections - which were whole-council elections held on new ward boundaries. With results in from 29 of the 30 new wards, Reform UK won 29 seats and have taken the council leadership: they will probably end up running a minority administration against 18 Conservatives, 17 Labour, 9 Greens, 9 councillors elected for the Your Bradford Independent Group which is the local Your Party franchise, 4 other independents and a single Lib Dem. Since the election one of the independent councillors has joined the Your Bradford Independent Group, while Reform UK councillor Daniel Devaney has quit the party to become an independent after being publicly busted for racism before the election; despite that, he still won. As we shall see, Devaney wasn’t the only Reform UK candidate to manage that dubious feat this year.

The three seats in Idle and Thackley ward are still to declare. This is Bradford’s Lib Dem hotspot, with the party having won every local election here for decades. In 2024 the Lib Dem lead here was 60-21 over Labour; the ward is basically unaffected by this year’s boundary changes.

Former Lib Dem councillors here included one David Ward, who was first elected as a Liberal/SDP Alliance councillor for the predecessor Idle ward all the way back in 1984. (He took over a seat vacated by the 1977-78 Lord Mayor of Bradford Paul Hockney, who was an older brother of the artist David Hockney.) Ward made several attempts to get into Parliament over the years, and he finally made it to the Commons in 2010 by gaining the Bradford East constituency from Labour. After a fiery and controversial term of office, in which he briefly lost the Lib Dem whip for offensive comments about Israel, David Ward lost his seat at the 2015 general election. He returned to Bradford council in 2016 as a Lib Dem councillor for the neighbouring Bolton and Undercliffe ward, but was then kicked out of the party shortly before the 2017 general election for antisemitism. Ward then sought re-election to the council in 2021 as an independent but lost his seat to Labour, returned in 2024 as an independent candidate in Bolton and Undercliffe ward, and then lost his seat there in May as a Your Bradford Independent Group candidate.

In the 2024 general election the Lib Dems finished in sixth place in Bradford East with 1,910 votes, only just saving their deposit and being beaten by the Greens, the Conservatives, Reform UK, an independent and Labour MP Imran Hussain, who has represented the seat since he defeated Ward in 2015. Hussain was one of the MPs who quickly lost the Labour whip in July 2024 for voting in favour of an SNP amendment to the King’s Speech to scrap the two-child benefit cap, but he is now back in the fold.

The 1,910 votes polled by the Lib Dems across the whole of the Bradford East constituency in July 2024 is less than the 2,499 votes which Lib Dem candidate Alun Griffiths polled in Idle and Thackley ward alone two months previously. He was re-elected on that occasion with a 60-21 lead over Labour. The ward is to all intents and purposes unaffected by this year’s boundary changes.

The three outgoing Lib Dem councillors for Idle and Thackley ward were Aislin Naylor who has served since 2022, retired GP Alun Griffiths who was first elected in 2006 and has continuous service from 2011, and political veteran Jeanette Sunderland who had been a Bradford councillor for over three decades, being first elected for the predecessor Idle ward back in 1994 and re-elected on eight further occasions. All three Idle and Thackley ward councillors had been nominated for re-election, but Sunderland died in April during the election campaign and this poll had to be postponed in consequence. She was 69 years old, and she had been diagnosed with cancer in 2024.

For this postponed poll outgoing councillors Griffiths and Naylor are joined on the Lib Dem slate by the replacement candidate Rachel Sunderland, who is Jeanette’s daughter. Rachel has served on Bradford council before, representing Bolton and Undercliffe ward from 2014 to 2018 and again from a February 2019 by-election to 2023. On the Labour slate in this by-election, Evelyne Godfrey is an archaeologist whose most recent election campaigns were in Canada, where she was an unsuccessful candidate for the New Democratic Party in the 2021 Canadian federal election and the 2024 New Brunswick provincial election; Gareth Logan was the Labour candidate for this ward in 2023 and 2024, finishing in a distant second place on both occasions; and Paul Wright appears to be a first-time candidate. The Conservatives have nominated David Bryant, Sally Cook (who gives an address over the border in Leeds) and Richard Wightman; the Green Party candidates Stuart Hurlbut, Melissa Jacobs and Tess Lawrence are clustered in the middle of the alphabetical ballot paper; and Reform UK are contesting this ward for the first time with their slate of Tom Macpherson le Maire, David Mills and John Riley. We now come to three polls in Essex, starting with another piece of unfinished business from May. Springfield is a north-eastern suburb of the city of Chelmsford, located to the east of the River Chelmer; the original Springfield village was annexed by Chelmsford in 1907, but there is still a Springfield parish which is now entirely built up with a 1970s housing estate. This is the Springfield which gave its name to all the Springfields in the USA, including the one in _The Simpsons_: William Pynchon, who went over to New England in the early 17th century, named the town of Springfield in Massachusetts after his former home village.

Law and order is a major industry here. The division includes the Essex police headquarters, the adjoining Essex police museum and HMP Chelmsford, a medium-security men’s prison. This was the filming location for the 1979 film version of _Porridge_ (not the TV series, which was made in the BBC studios); the prison was empty at the time of filming because it was being refurbished following a fire in one of the wings. The inmates at Chelmsford prison, of course, are not eligible to vote here.

Those who do vote here have tended to vote Liberal Democrat in recent years. The three wards of Chelmsford council which cover this division returned a full slate of Lib Dem councillors in 2023, and Springfield is also part of the Chelmsford parliamentary seat represented by Lib Dem MP Marie Goldman.

The predecessor Springfield division had been represented since 2005 by county councillor Mike Mackrory, who was leader of the Liberal Democrat opposition on Essex county council going into this election. He was a political veteran who had been first elected to Chelmsford council in 1995, and over the years Mackrory had served as mayor (1999-2000), council leader (2000-03) and opposition leader in Chelmsford. He suddenly died on 22nd April at the age of 80, in the middle of his election campaign to seek a sixth term of office on Essex county council; in consequence, the poll here had to be postponed. The rest of the county polled on 7th May as scheduled, and the new Essex county council has a large Reform UK majority: Reform UK won 53 out of the 77 seats that have already declared, with the Conservatives in second place on 13 and the Lib Dems reduced to 5. However, these figures have already changed as we shall see in the next section.

Mike Mackrory’s last win in Springfield division was in 2021, with a 46-37 lead over the Conservatives - curiously, this was exactly the same Lib Dem and Conservative scores as in 2017. This will not be directly comparable with today’s result because Essex county council got new division boundaries this year. The Springfield division has been reduced in size (it no longer covers all of Springfield North ward), while its name has had the word “Chelmsford” prepended to it.

The replacement Lib Dem candidate for Chelmsford Springfield is Richard Lee, who stood on 7th May in Braintree Town division and got nowhere; this should be a better prospect for him. The Tories have selected David Wilkinson, who works for a nature therapy and environmental charity. Also on the ballot are Adam Kenningham-Brown for Labour, Chris Rees for the Green Party and former social worker Tomy Sebastian for Reform UK. Votes here will be counted on Friday morning.

Both of these by-elections take place in the Essex town of Rayleigh, which is the main population centre in the Rochford local government district. In mediaeval times Rayleigh was a small town with a Norman motte-and-bailey castle, of which little remains, but housebuilding in the later 20th century and since has caused its population to balloon. Some recent development has spilled beyond the town boundaries into the parish of Rawreth, which separates Rayleigh from the town of Wickford to the west.

We now move into Greater London with the fourth and last postponed poll of the week, which is very much in Outer London. Hillingdon West ward lies to the east of Uxbridge town centre and is centred on the open space of Dowding Park, whose name is a clue to the area’s history. It’s a reference to Air Chief Marshal Hugh Dowding, who was the commander of RAF Fighter Command during the 1940 Battle of Britain.

Dowding Park lies on the site occupied until 2010 by RAF Uxbridge, which during the war years was the home of 11 Group RAF who were responsible for the aerial defence of London. The main operations room was underground, and it is now open to the public as a museum: the Battle of Britain Bunker has been restored in recent years with funding from central government and from Hillingdon council, which runs the place. Not far away from the bunker is the 19th-century mansion of Hillingdon House, whose grounds all this once were. Redevelopment work continues around the area, and Hillingdon council have plans to turn some derelict former RAF housing on the western side of the park into an extension of Uxbridge town centre.

Hillingdon council is run by the Conservatives, who have successfully defended their majority in this election. The 2022 result here was quite close with 30 Conservatives and 23 Labour councillors; this time round the Tories have won 30 seats against 16 Labour, 4 Reform UK and 1 Green, with the two seats in Hillingdon West ward to come. The election here was postponed after Sean Cooling, who was to have been a Reform UK candidate for the ward, died during the election campaign.

The Conservatives have a clear opportunity here to increase their council majority in the final reckoning. Hillingdon West was a safe Conservative ward when it was created for the 2022 election, with the Tories defeating Labour here on that occasion by 55-34. Before 2022 this area was mostly part of the larger Uxbridge North ward, which always voted Conservative in local elections. Nonetheless Labour might want to see how much of a fight they can put up here, because this ward is part of the Uxbridge and South Ruislip parliamentary seat whose Labour MP Danny Beales has a majority of just 587 votes from July 2024: Beales had been on the wrong side of a similar margin when he lost the parliamentary by-election here the previous year. Steve Tuckwell, the Conservative MP who Beales defeated in 2024, is now the Hillingdon council leader.

The two outgoing Conservative councillors for Hillingdon West are both seeking re-election. In the case of Reeta Chamdal the prize for winning is a big one: she was elected last month as the mayor of Hillingdon for 2026-27, a post which is presumably conditional on her getting back to the council in this poll. Her running-mate Adam Bennett has worked for over 20 years for British Airways, where he is currently head of Global Online Travel Agents. Bennett and Chamdal were both first elected in 2022. The Labour slate here consists of Tiffany Beales (who I think is the mother of Danny Beales MP) and Imran Razak, who are both first-time candidates. The only other party to stand here in 2022 was the Greens, who have taken advantage of the postponement to nominate a full slate with Alicia Windsor from the cancelled election joined by Ruhi Patel; on the Reform UK side Margaret Forrest remains from the original candidate list while Justin Anderson (who gives an address in faraway Portsmouth) has been nominated to replace the late Shaun Cooling; and the Lib Dem candidates of Muhammad Iqbal and Gautam Sabarwal complete a ballot paper of ten candidates. There are two seats available in this poll, and electors here have two votes.

_Lewisham council, London; caused by the election of Green Party councillor Liam Shrivastava as mayor of the borough._

Having got London’s postponed poll out of the way, we now travel south of the river to the first in a short series of London by-elections triggered by newly-elected Green Party councillors who were unable or unwilling to serve. In this case it’s a result of Liam Shrivastava being too successful at the polls in May and winning two elections at once: he became the fourth elected mayor of Lewisham, and he was also elected to Lewisham council as an ordinary councillor. [![Image 11](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ujlQ!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F91a08e09-cc49-4677-9adf-3413df7ef2fb_494x512.webp)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ujlQ!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F91a08e09-cc49-4677-9adf-3413df7ef2fb_494x512.webp)

Shrivastava was elected in 2022 as a Labour councillor for Lewisham’s New Cross ward before defecting to the Greens, but he didn’t seek re-election there. Instead we’re going to move two stops down the Windrush line to Honor Oak Park station, which lies on the western boundary of Lewisham borough and serves the western part of Crofton Park ward. The name Crofton Park was an invention of the London, Chatham and Dover Railway which opened Crofton Park station in 1892 on its Catford Loop line; before then the Crofton Park area in the north of this ward was considered to be part of Brockley. The largest open space in the ward is Blythe Hill Fields, a high point which has good views of east and south-east London. In the 2021 census Crofton Park was in the top 50 wards in England and Wales for people of mixed race (8.3%) and in the top 15 wards for residents employed in the arts, entertainment and recreation sector (7.2%).

Crofton Park ward was once the home of the Irish political activist Jim Connell, who wrote the socialist anthem _The Red Flag_ while on a train home to Honor Oak Park in 1889. Connell might well be pleased to note that his old stomping ground is a left-wing area in local elections, and - in common with Lewisham as a whole - Crofton Park ward had a full slate of Labour councillors from 2010 to 2026.

But this year the Labour redwash in Lewisham was broken in spectacular fashion, with the Green Party winning the borough’s mayoralty and an overall majority on the council, with 40 seats to Labour’s 14. Despite the fact that all three Green candidates were at the bottom of the ballot paper, Crofton Park ward followed suit with the Green slate defeating Labour by 52-31 - a swing of 18½% from Labour’s 49-33 win here four years ago.

This might well be causing some concern to this area’s Labour MP, although it would take a bigger Labour to Green swing to oust her. Crofton Park is part of the Lewisham West and East Dulwich constituency, which also takes in territory from Southwark borough to the west. In 2024 it was won by Ellie Reeves, who had represented the predecessor seat of Lewisham West and Penge since 2017. Reeves is a barrister who holds the post of Solicitor General, but she is not the most senior member of her family serving in government: she is the younger sister of Rachel Reeves, the Chancellor of the Exchequer.

As stated above, Liam Shrivastava’s election as mayor and councillor last month has opened up a vacancy on Lewisham council. Defending the resulting by-election for the Greens is Esther Lie, who currently works as a community organiser. Labour’s Alex Brooks was on their unsuccessful slate here in May and he is back for another go. Also standing are Richard Elliott for the Lib Dems, Caitlin Pugh for the Conservatives, Paul Newman for Reform UK and independent candidate Roger Mighton, who finished in eighth and last place in the Lewisham mayoral election last month.

## Bransgore, Burley, Sopley and Ringwood East

_New Forest council, Hampshire; caused by the resignation of Conservative councillor Richard Frampton._

We now travel from a ward in London which the Green Party gained at its last election, to a ward in Hampshire which the Green Party lost at its last election; from a Park which is full of houses, to a Forest which doesn’t really have many trees. That’s because the New Forest is a forest in the mediaeval sense of royal hunting territory, which encompassed both woodland and heathland. It’s in this heathland that we can find the village of Burley, located to the east of Ringwood around 13 miles north-east of Bournemouth.

Just outside the National Park boundary is Bransgore, whose eponymous parish includes a number of villages just outside Christchurch: Neacroft, Waterditch and Hinton are all part of this ward. Christchurch used to be part of Hampshire, but it was transferred to Dorset in the 1974 reorganisation; as part of that reorganisation the new Hampshire-Dorset boundary was drawn through the middle of what was then Christchurch East parish, and Bransgore parish is the part of that area which remained in Hampshire. The ward includes Hinton Admiral railway station on the northern edge of Christchurch’s built-up area. Not far from the station is the Office Field Solar Farm, which has been generating electricity for the National Grid since 2013.

To the west of Bransgore is the village of Sopley, which lies on the Hampshire Avon a few miles north of Christchurch. This was the home of a Second World War radar station and an associated RAF camp which was used in the 1970s to house Vietnamese boat people. Sopley is also the location of Moorlands College, which is a seminary for evangelical Christians. Finally, the Ringwood East part of the ward name is a reference to the eastern ward of the parish of Ringwood, which covers the area of Ringwood parish within the National Park boundary and doesn’t actually contain anything of the town itself: the main population centre here is the small village of Crow.

[![Image 12](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rw3n!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0c7bf623-5438-47b8-bb52-ef0feb495487_503x442.webp)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rw3n!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0c7bf623-5438-47b8-bb52-ef0feb495487_503x442.webp)

The 35 letters of “Bransgore, Burley, Sopley and Ringwood East” introduce one of the few genuinely rural wards in the New Forest district. This is because the New Forest district is generally not as rural as it might at first sound. In fact the New Forest is England’s second-largest second-tier district by population, after East Suffolk, and most of its residents live outside the national park in towns such as Ringwood in the Avon valley, Lymington, New Milton and other retirement towns on the coastal strip, the Southampton suburb of Totton and a very industrial area on the west bank of Southampton Water.

This ward was created in 2023 as a straight merger of the former Bransgore and Burley ward with the former Ringwood East and Sopley ward, with a reduction in the overall number of councillors from three to two but no cut to the number of elements in the ward name. The previous Bransgore and Burley ward was featured in this column in December 2021 as part of the fallout from a scandal involving the long-serving former Conservative leader of New Forest council Barry Rickman, who was prosecuted by the Environment Agency in 2021 for running a scrapyard without the necessary environmental permits and fined £1,000. Rickman was subsequently kicked out of the Conservative group on New Forest council, and the new council leader then proposed to remove him as one of the council’s representatives on the New Forest National Park Authority: that proposal led to the resignation of Bransgore and Burley ward councillor Mark Steele, who made complaints of bullying over the matter which were not upheld by the council’s monitoring officer. The resulting by-election, held two days before Christmas 2021, returned independent candidate and former ward councillor (2014-19) Richard Frampton who had previously sat on New Forest council for the both the Conservatives and the Lib Dems; the defending Conservative candidate actually fell to third place behind the Greens. There were no such shenanigans in the former Ringwood East and Sopley ward, which was very strongly Conservative to the point where it was left uncontested in 2015.

Two long-serving members of the Conservative awkward squad in the Commons, Sir Christopher Chope and Sir Desmond Swayne, live in this ward and are electors in this by-election. Sir Desmond has represented this area in Parliament since 1997 as part of the New Forest West constituency, and even in the carnage of 2024 he had no problem being re-elected for his eighth term of office.

Nonetheless the Conservative vote has been falling here in recent years. The Tories only just managed to keep control of New Forest council at the 2023 election, falling from 46 seats out of 60 to 26 out of 48 - a total which has since fallen to a minority of 23 out of 48, plus this vacancy, as a result of defection losses. Two of the New Forest Tory losses in 2023 came in Bransgore, Burley, Sopley and Ringwood East ward, which turned in a close three-way result. Independent candidate Nigel Linford finished top of the poll with 34%, and the other seat went to Neil Millington of the Green Party on 31%; the Conservatives finished close behind on 28%.

The Green Party councillor Neil Millington stepped down from New Forest council in December 2024 because he was moving away from the area. For the resulting Bransgore, Burley, Sopley and Ringwood East by-election in February 2025 the Conservatives selected Richard Frampton, who had won the 2014 Bransgore and Burley by-election for the Conservatives and the 2021 Bransgore and Burley by-election as an independent candidate - and Frampton did the hat-trick and easily gained the 2025 by-election from the Green Party. His lead over the Greens in the final reckoning was 60-19.

The most recent poll here was the 2026 Hampshire county council election, in which this ward is split between the Brockenhurst and Ringwood divisions. The Conservatives lost their majority on the county council this year, and one of the seats they lost was Ringwood which was gained by Reform UK; Brockenhurst, meanwhile, remained in Conservative hands. Richard Frampton resigned from New Forest council at about the same time, prompting the second Bransgore, Burley, Sopley and Ringwood East by-election of this term.

Defending for the Conservatives this time is Jan Sutherland, who is the vice-chair of Bransgore parish council. The Greens have reselected Barbara Czoch, a carpenter and foster carer who was their candidate in last year’s by-election. A rare all-female ballot paper is completed by Jannette Westgate of Reform UK, Hannah Phillips of the Lib Dems and Bronwen Bridges of Labour.

## Morriston; and  
Mumbles

_Swansea council, Glamorgan; caused respectively by the death of Labour councillor Robert Francis-Davies and by the the resignation of Francesca O’Brien._

The last seven of today’s polls take place in Wales, with all but one of them being a direct result of a recent law change by the Senedd. Welsh local government law has a general principle that you can only wear one political hat at once, so if you’re a councillor in Wales and you are elected to Westminster or to Senedd Cymru, then you are expected to resign your council position. There used to be an exemption from this rule for councillors who were in the last 53 weeks of their term, who would be allowed to see out their last year of office but would then be required to stand down at the following ordinary election. Since local elections in Wales take place a year after Senedd elections, this exemption saved quite a lot of hassle for newly-elected MSs. But the last Senedd abolished that exemption from May 2026 onwards, and we are now reaping the result of that change in the law. Nineteen of the 96 MSs elected in May were local councillors, and that means that 19 by-elections have now been triggered to add to the burden on electoral administrators, electors and this column. Six of those polls take place today, with the other 13 to follow over the coming weeks.

The first of those 19 new MSs we will feature here is Francesca O’Brien, who was top of the Reform UK list for the Gŵyr Abertawe constituency, which covers most of the Swansea council area, at the 2026 Senedd election. Reform UK won two of the six seats in Gŵyr Abertawe at that election, finishing in second place with 27% of the vote: Plaid Cymru topped the poll with 32% and won three seats, Labour won one seat with 14%, and the Conservatives were best of the rest on 10%. Gŵyr Abertawe covers both of the Swansea wards holding elections today.

[![Image 13](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ioyV!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe91f96df-9d5d-4d41-83c8-9e3fbe76b0fe_551x413.webp)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ioyV!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe91f96df-9d5d-4d41-83c8-9e3fbe76b0fe_551x413.webp)

O’Brien is a fairly recent recruit to Reform UK. She was elected to Swansea council in 2022 on the Conservative ticket, as a councillor for Mumbles ward. The headland known as the Mumbles is a beauty spot which lies at the western end of Swansea Bay: the land behind it is fairly heavily built up, with the villages of Langland, Newton and Oystermouth having fused together into a single urban area. Oystermouth is dominated by the impressive remains of a 13th-century castle, which is now in the care of Swansea council, while the beaches of western Swansea Bay and Langland Bay are a draw for day-trippers and holidaymakers on those occasions when the Welsh summer weather behaves itself.

Oystermouth is the final resting place of a man who died in 1825 but whose name lives on today in the English language. Thomas Bowdler has a chess attack named after him (1. e4 c5 2. Bc4, a reply by White to the Sicilian Defence which is now rarely seen at the top level), but he is mostly remembered as the publisher of _The Family Shakespeare_, “in which nothing is added to the original text; but those words and expressions are omitted which cannot with propriety be read aloud in a family”. What this meant in practice was the compilation of a censored edition of Shakespeare’s plays, with anything deemed too sexy, blasphemous or otherwise unsuitable for Georgian women and children to hear ruthlessly cut out. Ironically this censorship extended to the work’s authorship, as although Thomas Bowdler was credited on its title page the first edition of _The Family Shakespeare_ was in fact edited by his sister Harriet. Its commercial success led to Thomas spending the rest of his years compiling “Bowdlerised” editions of other works, including a family-friendly version of Gibbons’ _Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire_ which was unfinished when he died and was completed by his nephew. Bowdler set off a whole genre of expurgated literary works which were popular and generally seen as a Good Thing in the nineteenth century, and it wasn’t until the First World War years that the term “bowdlerisation” started to take on connotations of unwelcome censorship. But in these days of mooted social media bans for children, maybe Thomas Bowdler’s legacy is starting to come fashionable again?

[![Image 14](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Lzyc!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb568b5b3-6706-43c6-92f0-a706ab9554e1_461x551.webp)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Lzyc!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb568b5b3-6706-43c6-92f0-a706ab9554e1_461x551.webp)

The Mumbles area is still populated by the sort of affluent middle-class families who would have enjoyed Bowdler’s work back in the day. Rather different in character is Morriston, a planned industrial village in northern Swansea which was built for and named after the industrialist Sir John Morris in the late eighteenth century. This is the core of the Morriston electoral ward, which extends along the west back of the River Tawe to take in the villages of Cwmrhydyceirw and Ynystawe. The ward’s largest employer is Morriston Hospital, where many of Swansea’s residents begin and end their lives. Although the Swansea offices of the DVLA are often described as being in Morriston, the DVLA complex is in fact located to the west of here in Mynydd-bach ward; nevertheless it has an effect on Morriston’s census return, with the ward making the top 100 in England and Wales for those working in administrative and secretarial occupations (13.6%).

[![Image 15: Swansea, 2022](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Tsyo!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd671d2a8-9af4-4604-896b-7bb61ee9e7e4_1050x800.svg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Tsyo!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd671d2a8-9af4-4604-896b-7bb61ee9e7e4_1050x800.svg)

Morriston is a very large electoral ward which elects five Swansea councillors by first-past-the-post - something which would not be tolerated in England, where the Local Government Boundary Commission caps the size of wards at three councillors. In the 2022 Swansea council election the Labour slate here was guaranteed one of the five seats because only four opposition candidates stood, and Labour went on to elect all five councillors very easily with a 61-15 lead over the Conservatives. This places Morriston within the Labour majority on Swansea council.

At Westminster Morriston is part of the Swansea West constituency, which has only had three MPs - all Labour - in the last 60 years. Alan Williams retired in 2010 as Father of the House, with continuous service from 1964. His successor Geraint Davies represented the seat as a Labour MP for 13 years before being suspended from the party in 2023 over sexual harassment allegations. The Labour party’s investigation into this never seems to have reached a conclusion, and Davies was effectively forced into retirement as he was still outside the fold when the 2024 general election was called. His successor is a Labour Party high-flyer: Torsten Bell came to the Commons in 2024 from nine years running the Resolution Foundation economic thinktank, and he has brought that work into government as a junior Treasury and DWP minister.

The Mumbles ward makes the top 40 in England and Wales for residents in lower managerial, administrative and professional occupations (28.6%). It was created in 2022 as a merger of the previous single-member Newton and Oystermouth wards, plus territory transferred from West Cross ward to the north, with an increase in the overall number of councillors from two to three. Newton and Oystermouth had both returned Conservative councillors for some years previously, and Mumbles continued in that vein in 2022 by giving 42% to the winning Conservative slate, 29% to Labour and 13% to the Greens.

This ward is part of the Gower Westminster constituency, which has been represented since 2017 by the chair of the Northern Ireland Affairs committee Tonia Antoniazzi. In 2019 she narrowly defeated Conservative candidate Francesca O’Brien, who was subsequently elected in 2022 as a Conservative councillor for Mumbles ward before defecting to Reform UK in 2025. O’Brien has now left Swansea council after her election to the Senedd last month, and she has slotted straight onto the Reform UK frontbench in Cardiff Bay as shadow cabinet member for local government, housing and planning.

Today’s other by-election is to replace Swansea’s longest-serving local councillor. Robert Francis-Davies was first elected all the way back in 1983, giving 43 years of unbroken service as a councillor for Morriston. He was Lord Mayor of the city in 2001-02, and he was active in local government right up to the end as the Swansea cabinet member for investment, regeneration, tourism and events. It was a job Francis-Davies had clearly excelled at over many years, with the council leader’s tribute noting his contribution to the planning of the Swansea.com Stadium (home of Swansea City FC) and the National Waterfront Museum, together with bringing events such as Proms in the Park to Swansea. Robert Francis-Davies died in May at the age of 78, with the coroner’s inquest attributing his death to a combination of renal cancer and a fall from a mobility scooter.

The defending Labour candidate in the by-election to replace Robert Francis-Davies is his daughter Rebecca, an HR consultant who was in fourth place on the Labour list for Gŵyr Abertawe last month; in the 2022 Swansea elections she contested Uplands ward. Another unsuccessful Senedd candidate who is straight back on the campaign trail is the Conservatives’ Idin Ghotbi, who made up the numbers in sixth and last place on the Conservative list for Gŵyr Abertawe. The Lib Dem candidate is Hayden Lewis, Reform UK have selected Graham Ashby, Gareth Schofield is the Green candidate and Ioan Warlow stands for Plaid Cymru.

In Mumbles ward Reform UK will want to convert their defection gain into a by-election gain, and hoping to do that is their candidate Emilie Cox: she was an unsuccessful Conservative candidate in the 2022 Swansea elections, finishing as runner-up behind Labour in the neighbouring West Cross ward. The Conservatives will want to recover their loss and they have selected Hannah Williams. Standing for Labour is David Lewis, who sits on Mumbles community council and runs a B&B in the ward. The Green candidate Rich Williams has had a long career in the commercial and charity sector, and he currently runs a Swansea youth work charity. Also on the Mumbles ballot are Plaid Cymru’s Tricia Sanderson who was an unsuccessful candidate here in 2022, the Lib Dems’ Jim Hehir who stood for the Senedd last month in Afan Ogwr Rhondda, and independent candidate Dorian Davies who stood in Oystermouth ward back in 2017 and lists current membership of Reform UK on his nomination papers. Intending Conservative and Green voters should check carefully which Williams they are voting for.

## Acton and Maesydre;  
Grosvenor; and  
Queensway

_Wrexham council, North Wales; caused respectively by the resignations of Plaid Cymru councillors Becca Martin, Marc Jones and Carrie Harper._

We now come to the largest settlement in North Wales, the city of Wrexham, where three by-elections are taking place to replace Plaid Cymru councillors who have all been elected to Senedd Cymru. In May Carrie Harper and Marc Jones were the top two candidates on the Plaid list for the Fflint Wrecsam constituency which covers Wrexham, where the main nationalist party polled 26% of the vote and won two out of six seats; while Becca Martin was elected in second place on the Plaid Cymru list for Clwyd, which scored 28% and won two seats. Reform UK were first in both constituencies, and in the first-past-the-post context of these by-elections that’s all-important.

[![Image 16](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!anPG!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe73c2e50-d865-4fcd-8e77-f79be5519663_548x440.webp)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!anPG!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe73c2e50-d865-4fcd-8e77-f79be5519663_548x440.webp)

The three outgoing Plaid councillors all represented urban wards in Wrexham proper. Carrie Harper’s ward was Queensway, which is in the east of the city and is one of the five wards covering the massive Caia Park housing estate, whose utterly working-class population drives a remarkable census return. This ward has 31.0% of its population aged under 16: that is the highest figure for any ward in Wales, and only four wards in England (two covering areas of new development in the Thames estuary, and two covering the Jewish enclave in northern Hackney) are higher. Queensway also has the second-highest proportion of social housing in England and Wales at 70.4% of households, behind only Acrefair North ward elsewhere in Wrexham; it also makes the top 100 wards in England and Wales for households living rent-free (0.9%), for adults with no qualifications (35.5%), for adults with between 1 and 4 GCSEs or equivalent (14.2%, the highest figure in Wales), for adults who are looking after home or family (12.3%, the highest figure in Wales), for adults who are long-term sick or disabled (12.2%), for residents employed in manufacturing (18.3%), for residents employed in administrative and support service activities (9.2%, the highest figure in Wales), for semi-routine occupations (19.5%) and for routine occupations (25.1%). This is not a result of immigration: the ward is only 5% non-white with 11% of the the population born outside the UK. Harper was first elected for the ward in 2017, and she won a second term of office in 2022 with a thumping 75-22 lead over Labour.

[![Image 17](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!C6EO!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9a56a1da-6a7a-4dcd-bb35-04c2fbd2b1b5_471x481.webp)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!C6EO!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9a56a1da-6a7a-4dcd-bb35-04c2fbd2b1b5_471x481.webp)

Also first elected in 2017 was Marc Jones, who was re-elected in 2022 in Grosvenor ward with a 63-26 lead over Labour. Most of this ward’s residents live in the Rhosddu area immediately to the north of the city centre; the name of Grosvenor ward is a reference to the Dukes of Westminster, who we met in last week’s Preview. This ward covers a large chunk of Wrexham city centre, including the Guildhall which is the home of Wrexham council, and it extends north-westwards to take in Wrexham General railway station, the main campus of Wrexham University, and the Racecourse Ground football stadium.

The Racecourse Ground is the home of Wrexham AFC, who have gained a new fanbase and success in recent years thanks to their ownership by US actors Rob McElhinney and Ryan Reynolds. The stadium also claims to be the oldest international football ground in the world. The Welsh national team played their first home match here in 1877, losing 2-0 to Scotland, and the Racecourse Ground has hosted more Wales matches through the years than any other venue. But these days the Cardiff City Stadium is the national football team’s permanent home, and Wales’ last match at the Racecourse was a low-profile friendly against Gibraltar in 2023.

[![Image 18](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!frne!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2eb33dfe-2b3b-4573-b0ef-74139b35a158_484x544.webp)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!frne!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2eb33dfe-2b3b-4573-b0ef-74139b35a158_484x544.webp)

The third Wrexham councillor departing for Cardiff Bay is Becca Martin, who last appeared in this column when she won a March 2021 by-election for Maesydre ward which lies immediately north-east of the city centre. It’s fair to say that I didn’t see that result coming: Plaid had not previously stood a candidate in Maesydre ward this century. Boundary changes for the 2022 election merged Maesydre with Acton ward to the north, creating a two-seat ward of Acton and Maesydre which split its representation between Plaid and Labour: Plaid Cymru polled 37% to 26% for Labour and 22% for an independent candidate. In the 2021 census Acton and Maesydre made the top 100 wards in England and Wales for residents employed in manufacturing (18.1%).

The northern end of Acton and Maesydre ward is covered by the open space of Acton Park, which was once the grounds of Acton Hall before its demolition in the 1950s. Acton Hall was the birthplace of George Jeffreys, the notorious hanging judge who was James II’s Lord Chancellor and presided over the “Bloody Assizes” of 1685. The park includes Britain’s Tree of the Year for 2023, a sweet chestnut tree which is nearly 500 years old; also here is a stone circle, commemorating the visit of the National Eisteddfod to Wrexham in 1977.

[![Image 19: Wrexham, 2022](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!iCkv!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc938d465-038a-4a10-939d-873e9b73d8bd_1400x941.svg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!iCkv!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc938d465-038a-4a10-939d-873e9b73d8bd_1400x941.svg)

Harper, Jones and Martin were a large chunk of the Plaid Cymru group on Wrexham council, which has a plurality of independent councillors. The 2022 elections here returned 23 independents, 14 Labour, 9 Conservatives, 9 Plaid and a Lib Dem councillor; the main independent group heads a coalition which also includes the Conservatives and the Lib Dem. All this is rather different to the 2024 Westminster election in the Wrexham constituency, which was a rather easy gain for Labour: the town’s MP is Andrew Ranger, who has spent most of his career working in hospitality.

On the basis of the previous results Plaid Cymru might be most worried about Acton and Maesydre. Their defending candidate in that ward is Richard Everall, a long-serving former fireman who was also a Fire Brigades Union rep. Labour have selected Salli Edwards, who runs the Flintshire branch of Citizens Advice. We have an independent candidacy from Alex Jones, who was an independent candidate for the city’s Erddig ward in 2017 and 2022. The Conservatives have selected Will Martin, Natasha Morris stands for the Greens, Reform UK’s nominee is Jan Davey, and the Lib Dems’ Beatrice Williams is last on the Acton and Maesydre ballot paper.

The Grosvenor by-election is defended for Plaid by first-time candidate Jonathan Billington. Here the Labour candidate is Brendan Murray who is a driving instructor. Beth Vaughan stands in Grosvenor ward for the Conservatives, Graham Bannister-Kelly for the Greens, Gerald Craddock for the Lib Dems, former community councillor Philip Penk for Reform UK, Sam Regan - who owns and runs a hotel in the city - is standing here as an independent candidate, and Martine Richards makes a bit of electoral history as the first-ever council by-election candidate for Your Party.

For their defence of the Queensway by-election Plaid Cymru have decided to ignore the usual stereotypes by selecting Pol Wong, a 33rd-generation Shaolin monk who makes a living by teaching kung fu. Wong, whose father Jummy opened and ran the first Chinese restaurant in North Wales, was last seen on a ballot paper in 2017 when he stood in Ruabon ward. The Labour candidate Morgan Peters is a Caia Park community councillor who stood on the party’s list in Gwynedd Maldwyn at the recent Senedd election. Also contesting Queensway ward are Geoffrey Sutton for the Conservatives, Robbie Green for Reform UK and Lucy Sutton for the Greens. Intending Conservative and Green voters should check carefully which Sutton they are voting for.

Tudno

_Conwy council, North Wales; caused respectively by the resignations of Louise Emery and Thomas Montgomery._

We’ll finish for the week on the seaside, in the Costa Geriatrica of North Wales. Roughly at the centre of the North Wales coast we find the town of Llandudno, which lies on low ground between the twin headlands of the Little Orme and the Great Orme. The town has two beaches, one facing north into the Irish Sea and the other facing west into the mouth of the River Conwy.

Orme is a Norse name, an unusual feature in North Wales, which refers to a sea serpent and is from the same root which gave us the English word “worm”. The craggy limestone of the Great Orme rises to a summit of 207 metres and it is classed as a Marilyn, a British peak which rises at least 150 metres above the surrounding landscape. Its highest point is occupied by a visitor centre, which was once a semaphore station passing messages between Holyhead and Liverpool. This is an excellent viewpoint for the Irish Sea, with views extending on a good day to the Isle of Man and the Lake District; theoretically the summit of Slieve Donard, 103 miles away in Northern Ireland, is also visible from here.

The summit complex is adjacent to the terminus of the Great Orme Tramway, which runs down the steep slope into the town centre. This is operated as two separate funicular railways, meaning that all passengers must change trams at the Halfway station. The lower section of the Tramway runs along public streets to reach its lower terminus.

Not far away from here are the remains of copper mines on the Great Orme which go all the way back to the Bronze Age: metallurgical analysis has demonstrated that during the period 1600 to 1400 BC the Great Orme was the main source of copper in Britain. Also up here on the headland we find a small church dedicated to St Tudno, an obscure saint who lived as a hermit on the Great Orme in the sixth century. This is the church of St Tudno which gives its name to the town of Llandudno below.

Llandudno as we know it today is a creation of the Victorians, who turned it from a copper-mining centre into a seaside resort, and the North Promenade in particular is wall-to-wall Victorian hotels. Behind those hotels we find the town centre, whose main shopping street is Mostyn Street which runs parallel to the North Promenade: this is named after Lord Mostyn, who still owns large chunks of Llandudno to this day.

Holidaymakers here back in the day included Alice Pleasance Liddell, the inspiration for Lewis Carroll’s _Alice_ novels. To mark this connection a series of statues of characters from _Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland_ and _Through the Looking Glass_ have been erected in the town - this trend started with a depiction of the White Rabbit on Mostyn Street, which was unveiled by Llandudno’s then MP David Lloyd George all the way back in 1933. The annual Victorian Extravaganza, which is normally held over the May bank holiday weekend so you’ve missed it for this year, is quite the experience.

[![Image 20](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fxNb!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe8680102-d7e9-49e7-b112-9b87573b2e84_549x462.webp)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fxNb!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe8680102-d7e9-49e7-b112-9b87573b2e84_549x462.webp)

The Gogarth Mostyn ward of Conwy covers Llandudno’s town centre, the western shore and the Great Orme. This ward also includes the town’s railway station, which lies at the end of a branch off the North Wales Coast line.

[![Image 21](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Kdk1!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1cee8309-ca83-405d-a160-6d725d67e663_475x552.webp)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Kdk1!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1cee8309-ca83-405d-a160-6d725d67e663_475x552.webp)

Immediately to the east of here is Tudno ward, where we find the theatre and conference centre of Venue Cymru on the North Promenade. This is the regular location for the Welsh Open snooker tournament, and it also hosts politicians from time to time. The Welsh Conservative conference was held at Venue Cymru in February, and Plaid Cymru have pencilled Llandudno in as the location for their next party conference in October.

The boundary between Tudno and Gogarth Mostyn wards runs along Vaughan Street, and the T-junction of Vaughan Street and the North Promenade marks the northern end of the A470 road which winds its merry way down the length of Wales to the Senedd building at Cardiff Bay. Today’s by-elections in both of those wards, which between them cover nearly all of Llandudno town, are both caused by Conwy councillors being elected to Senedd Cymru in May. Louise Emery and Thomas Montgomery were respectively ranked second and third on the Reform UK list for the Clwyd constituency, which polled 32% of the vote and won three out of six seats.

Emery and Montgomery are both relatively recent recruits to Reform UK, and they were originally elected to Conwy council on the Conservative ticket. Louise Emery was first elected in 2017 for Gogarth ward which then covered the Great Orme and the west shore, gaining her seat from an independent councillor. Boundary changes for 2022 then merged Gogarth with the town-centre Mostyn ward, and the combined ward turned in a close result with 36% for Labour, 34% for the Conservatives and 30% for independent candidates; the three seats split one to Labour and two to the Conservatives. Thomas Montgomery was in his first term as a councillor for Tudno ward, which in 2022 voted 31% for Labour, 29% for the Conservatives, 25% for independent candidates and 16% for the Liberal Democrats; Labour had only stood one candidate, leaving Montgomery to win the second seat on the Conservative ticket.

[![Image 22: Conwy, 2022](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!mT7m!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7c2fd4d6-4a3f-44c4-ba56-f95baa9e43c2_700x800.svg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!mT7m!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7c2fd4d6-4a3f-44c4-ba56-f95baa9e43c2_700x800.svg)

Those results were unusually party political for Conwy council, where independent councillors are the largest group and lead the administration. The 2022 Conwy election returned 22 independent councillors, 11 Labour, 10 Conservatives, 7 Plaid Cymru (most of whom were elected from wards in the interior), 4 Lib Dems and a single Green councillor. These are the first by-elections of the present Conwy council term.

Llandudno is one of the major towns in the Westminster seat of Bangor Aberconwy, which was won in 2024 by Labour candidate Claire Hughes. For Senedd purposes that seat is combined with the Isle of Anglesey to form a rather undersized constituency of Bangor Conwy Môn: in May this constituency gave 45% and three seats to Plaid Cymru, 28% and two seats to Reform UK, and 12% and one seat to the Conservatives. Top of the Plaid Cymru list here was their party leader, and now the First Minister of Wales, Rhun ap Iorwerth. Local elections in Wales are not a particularly reliable indicator of party support, but it’s fair to say that Plaid Cymru’s strength in this constituency lies outside Llandudno. Neither of these by-elections has a Plaid candidate.

Whether this means that Reform UK can convert their defection gains into by-election gains remains to be seen. In Gogarth Mostyn the new Reform UK candidate is Gareth Probert, a Conwy town councillor who has recently defected to the party from the Conservatives. The Tories have selected Greg Robbins, who is trying to get back on Conwy council after losing his seat here in 2022: Robbins had represented the former Mostyn ward from 2017 to 2022, and he still sits on Llandudno town council and has served as mayor of the town more than once. He previously appeared in this column as the losing Conservative candidate for a Mostyn ward by-election in 2016. Labour’s David Hawkins is a Llandudno town councillor for Mostyn ward, and he is married to this year’s mayor Mandy Hawkins. There are no independent candidates this time, but Dave Coffin completes an all-male ballot for the Lib Dems.

Finally for this week, we come to the Tudno ward by-election where the Reform UK candidate is Alan Davies. The Tories will want their seat back and they have selected Michael Hall. Standing for Labour is Joanna Stallard, who was top of the Labour list for Bangor Conwy Môn in May; she also stood in the 2024 general election in Dwyfor Meirionnydd. Again there is no independent challenge this time. The Lib Dems are back with James Pethica, who gives an address in Rhos-on-Sea and runs a business selling climbing-related jewellery, and this time we also have an intervention from the Greens whose candidate is Joshua Morris.

This has been an exceptionally long Preview; but if anything, next week will be even busier with 23 local council seats up for grabs on 25th June. You won’t want to miss that.

**His name has been a fixture on Christchurch voting papers for more than half a century, and his election booklet blurbs are considered by some to be ‘[precious works of art](https://thespinoff.co.nz/local-elections/25-09-2019/tubby-hansens-voting-booklet-blurbs-are-precious-works-of-art)‘. Who is the mysterious Tubby Hansen?**

_This story was first published on[Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/health/300631037/another-health-crisis-is-coming-but-families-dont-want-to-hear-about-childhood-vaccines)._

On a tidy suburban street in south Christchurch, one house stands out.

The weatherboards are painted in lilac and yellow stripes, while the window frames are pink. A truck parked in the driveway has four flat tyres and is streaked with rust and mildew. The cabin is filled with polystyrene packaging and the flatbed is loaded with branches.

On the front lawn stands a small wooden billboard that offers a clue to the man who lives in this house. The billboard is painted grey, but features the handwritten slogan “Progressive nudist for Spreydon ward councillor. Vote Tubby.”

The man who lives in this house is called Tubby Hansen and he is a bit of a local character. He has stood in every [general election and mayoral race](https://www.stuff.co.nz/the-press/news/129716000/a-wizard-a-pastor-and-two-retirees-are-among-the-lesserknown-candidates-vying-for-christchurchs-mayoralty) in Christchurch since 1969. Over more than five decades and 34 elections, he has attracted a grand total of 9,468 votes. In one general election he got 10 votes.

![Image 6: The Daily](blob:http://localhost/b9a31d3949b1882a09ed2f8508d538f3)

Hansen’s candidate photographs from the 1971 mayoral election, left, the 1980 campaign and in 1998.

During every election he runs ads in The Press newspaper. Some outline his ideas for the city, like a [limit on house prices](https://www.stuff.co.nz/life-style/homed/real-estate/123882486/affordability-crunch-will-house-prices-hit-a-limit) and replacing the “inhumane” metal seats in bus shelters. But other ads feature nightmarish stories about the use of an “X-ray electronic cruelty machine” to sting people, a “tingle ray” deployed at council meetings, and [surveillance bugs hidden in radios](https://www.stuff.co.nz/technology/126681533/privacy-online-the-endless-creep-of-surveillance).

After each election, he runs an ad personally thanking the handful of people who voted for him.

But who is Tubby Hansen? And why has he run for office so many times? I knock on his front door to find out.

It takes a while for him to come to the door and open all the various locks. But once the door swings open, there is Hansen wearing a black top and tracksuit trousers with white hair and a neat beard. Behind him we can see a lawnmower in his hallway and a chaos of papers and boxes.

He smiles when he hears I am from Stuff and is happy to chat. He walks with a stick to his front lawn and asks me to grab a plastic chair for him to sit on.

He immediately begins complaining about his swollen knee.

“I haven’t hurt my knee,’’ he says. “I can tell the police about it, but I can’t tell you publicly. But I can say that I am being masered​ on the knee.”

He calmly explains that a maser​ is an electro-magnetic laser that is being used to target his knee at night. “It is an invisible ray. The political left is trying to stop me. They try to stop me with their bloody masers and interfering with my truck.”

He thinks his truck is being sabotaged? “If they can cause constant repairs it gobbles up my savings and then I can’t run in the elections.”

We both look at his forlorn-looking truck. I suggest it might have bigger problems than sabotage. “It would work if it was put right,’’ he says.

![Image 8: The Daily](blob:http://localhost/b9a31d3949b1882a09ed2f8508d538f3)

Tubby Hansen has stood in every Christchurch election since 1969 (Photo: Alden Williams/Stuff)

So, why has he stood in so many elections? “I like to raise issues that the other candidates don’t.”

I ask what kind of issues, and he talks about a new development on Lincoln Road in Addington that has a dangerously narrow footpath.

Talking to Hansen feels similar to reading his election ads and campaign material. He flips from the fantastical to the everyday with uncanny comic timing. His 2004 mayoral pitch, included in the information pack that comes with voting papers, is a classic example:

“The use of a stingray [sic], and a tingle ray at election meetings and a very hot ray which can pass through walls is not acceptable, candidates should have the use of a council car.”

In one pitch, when standing for the Canterbury District Health Board in 2019, Hansen describes how a team of people bugged a man’s “radio, jug, urn and fan heater”. The disturbing story ends with the line:

“Something must be done about the thrush and [chlamydia boom](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/health/127715517/you-may-have-chlamydia-email-from-university-of-otago-an-uncomfortable-but-welcome-surprise).”

![Image 10: The Daily](blob:http://localhost/b9a31d3949b1882a09ed2f8508d538f3)

Hansen’s candidate photographs for Christchurch elections in 1979, left, 1986 and 1989.

Hansen says he pays for the ads by saving his pension over the three years between elections. The 77-year-old is now retired after working at the freezing works, Temuka Pottery, the Christchurch gasworks, a nail factory and many others places. His father worked on the railways and so his childhood was spent roving across New Zealand, before settling in Christchurch in 1961.

A story in The Press from 1966 describes how Hansen, then 20, was remanded to [Sunnyside psychiatric hospital](https://www.stuff.co.nz/the-press/editors-picks/7208909/Mental-healthcare-moves-out-of-hospital) after a charge of assault. Hansen says it happened after a fight with his father.

“My father was a drunken, violent man. He came home at Christmas and he was drunk. His attitude was he had parental control over me and could punch me. I punched back and he put a charge on me and they sent me to Sunnyside. I used to intervene between him and Mum and he came to resent me. I am pleased he is dead now.”

Has he stayed at a psychiatric hospital since then? He folds his arms, looks away and says: “Not really, no.”

As we talk on his front lawn a tabby cat wanders over to greet Hansen. “This is Chloe from over the road.” They clearly like each other. She rubs around his legs as we talk about happier times.

![Image 12: The Daily](blob:http://localhost/b9a31d3949b1882a09ed2f8508d538f3)

Tubby Hansen greets the neighbour’s cat, Chloe (Photo: Alden Williams/Stuff)

He talks with a wry smile about the fun of the election trail. He enjoys the sense of connection at public election meetings. “You have a bit of fun. People laugh.”

How does he fancy his chances in his 18th Christchurch mayoral race this year? “I think [Phil Mauger](https://www.stuff.co.nz/the-press/news/129690818/phil-mauger--who-styles-himself-as-the-peoples-councillor--on-a-different-form-of-leadership-and-cutting-down-bureaucracy) will win this one because he started his advertising programme early.” He smiles and adds: “But only if I don’t get in as mayor.”

Does he really think he could win?

“Robert the Bruce said: ‘Try, try and try again’.”

Christchurch

![Image 18: The Beehive with staff lanyard](https://images.thespinoff.co.nz/1/2026/09/Parliament-Staff.png?w=1290&fm=auto&auto=compress%2Cformat)

For political staff, election year is as close as you get to a performance review.

Political staff have a reputation for being self-important panic merchants. Sometimes it’s a valid criticism. More often, it’s because the people they advise are important and the jobs they do are genuinely stressful.

If you hate performance management, professional development courses, clunky leave portals, or the daily quiz, become a political staffer; you’ll be bothered by none of that in these roles.

The job of a political staffer is fundamentally different to that of a public servant. Not just on paper but in terms of expectations and working conditions. Shortly, parliament will see a whole new intake of political staff, and likely some new-entrant politicians.

My first role for Parliamentary Services started in 2008, near on my 21st birthday. I worked for two MPs, two leaders of the opposition, one prime minister and have since worked as a freelance advisor on resources like induction handbooks for press secretaries and political advisors.

The newbies will soon learn the parliamentary precinct is a peculiar place to work. There are bars and restaurants on-site, a pool, a gym, portraits of past prime ministers that loom large in the corridors and a 4,500-strong art collection including a lock of Queen [Victoria’s hair](https://www.facebook.com/watch/?v=2427654224298429).

The job takes you to every corner of the country and sometimes overseas where you get the opportunity to truly work 24/7. It’s this promise of glitz and glam that has sustained some pretty unhealthy work habits over the years.

For political staff – present and aspiring – election year is as close as you get to a performance review. For those in opposition, moving over to the Beehive is a journey to the promised land, and not everyone will make it. For beltway escapees, the pull to return can often be ignored until someone else convinces you to come back. It’s almost always ill-advised. And for new entrants, there’s an induction folder somewhere in the bowels of the Department of Internal Affairs that will tell you next to nothing about the realities of your role.

As a political staffer, your brain will become cloud storage for your member of parliament. You will be the custodian of their political agenda, troubleshooter-in-chief, timekeeper and listening ear.

You will need to manage conflicting priorities and personalities so your MP doesn’t have to. You are paid to ensure your MP’s time isn’t monopolised and that all work that reaches them is of a high standard. You are there to ensure they are never surprised.

That does not mean you will never be surprised. Spare a thought for the staff of recently ousted National Party minister Chris Penk… there are some circumstances you just can’t get ahead of.

I’ve got a genuine interest in improving the working lives of the people who prop up our politicians, and recently I spoke to Professor Jennifer Lees-Marshment, from the University of Dundee, about what New Zealand might do differently to better manage the talent of aspiring and experienced political staff and their transition between administrations. We’d met when she interviewed me for her book; [The Human Resource Management of Political Staffers](https://www.taylorfrancis.com/books/mono/10.4324/9781032636429/human-resource-management-political-staffers-jennifer-lees-marshment).

Lees-Marshment has studied political staff working in the UK, New Zealand, Australian and Canadian Parliaments. She says that the picture is muddy and no country has yet got it right. Political staff abroad face sub-standard working conditions including limited or absent HR processes, ineffective orientation, a lack of fit-for-purpose training, and deficient performance management. She also cites rising mental health problems including high burnout.

“The findings were so stark I published advisors’ descriptions of their workplaces in their own words,” says Lees-Marshment.

These [included](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/09540962.2025.2540466):

*   “It always felt like everything was on fire.”
*   “Sometimes it feels almost like some sort of 18th-century feudal system”
*   “The Hunger Games”
*   “I was a director at 26. I had never been a director before, and I never got formal training to be a director.”
*   “You’re never not at work.”

She says the work of political staff is often misunderstood: “Unlike permanent public servants, political staff have no job security, do not have clear performance management or rewards, and often lack even basic rights that other professions take for granted.”

One reason these jobs are so precarious is the events-based contract that ties a staffer to their MP or minister personally, in an antiquated employment relationship that can resemble a bad marriage. You could consider the events-based contract as the one thing that sets the political staffer apart. But that would be missing the point. The work of political staff is events-based, there is no getting around that. But there is plenty that could be improved between coups, elections, and political falls from grace.

Lees-Marshment points out there is a large-scale bureaucratic infrastructure to support public servants. Political staff get nothing in comparison, and it is “deeply unfair”.

“The job of a political staffer requires high levels of agility and learning at speed without appropriate training; they have to work much longer hours, including being contactable in the evenings, weekends and even at night time; they are under significant public scrutiny where something small going wrong can end up on the evening news.”

I saw the insecurity, pressure and intensity bubble up in novel ways. I remember a group of opposition staff being reprimanded for actual sword fighting one night. I doubt it was in defence of the honour of one of their MPs… but ceremonial swords were swung about the office. Politics can be cut-throat.

Unless you do something genuinely stupid, the job of a political staffer is unusual in that your career trajectory is largely out of your control.

“Political staff know that even if their politician is re-elected, decisions about what position they might occupy are influenced by lots of things that have little to do with their performance,” Lees-Marshment says.

Lees-Marshment recommends an Office for Political Staff. “We’d keep the best political staffers in the system which is good for individuals but also good for democracy,” Lees-Marshment says.

An Office for Political Staff would oversee a more rigorous selection process. The office would not only provide politicians with pre-assessed candidates to choose from (Ministerial and Parliamentary Services have made gains in this space) but give political staff themselves a bit of dignity, like that their value exists beyond their current contract.

Right now, if you want to continue in a political role you have the option of putting your CV into this faceless electronic pot of people from where it may or may not be plucked, by who knows who, for who knows what. When you’ve put your life on hold for a political job, it’s a thankless place to end up every three years.

Detractors argue that when politics, power and control are involved, no new office is going to make a difference.

“Few would argue that we couldn’t do things better,” Lees-Marshment says.

“No one is suggesting an Office for Political Staff would remove politicians’ choice – they would always make the final decisions. But we could look after people better and keep people in the profession longer.”

The reality for political staff seems to be to work yourself into the ground and hope for the best.

“It frustrates me that there are so many reviews and organisational change programmes focusing on public policy and public servants, as if that is why government does not work. But the missing link is looking at how politics works.”

“You could take anyone, even the most clever and capable person, and drop them into these high-pressured public facing roles, without training, where they are expected to perform from day one, without appropriate support and management, and they would struggle. At the very least, they cannot reach their full potential. At their worst, the stress they experience hinders good decision making.”

Parliamentary Services chief executive Rafael Gonzalez-Montero, however, says New Zealand political staff are looked after as there’s “a team dedicated to ensuring members, and the staff who support them, receive personalised, high-quality services, and support aligned with their needs”.

“Professional supervision is also offered which provides staff an additional avenue for professional reflection, support, and development. Staff have access to a range of wellbeing support, including the Employee Assistance Programme which provides confidential counselling and wellbeing support for employees and their families,” he says.

Gonzalez-Montero says additional support is provided during the election period.

Just as well. With the election fast approaching, politicians will be running a ruler over their staff. Some will have signalled they’re over it, burnt out, not willing to do another turn through the revolving door. Others will be fiercely loyal, competent and accustomed to the rigour of the roles. But it’s the political newbies I have my eye on. I’m sure we can do better by these energised people, and we should.
